# Methods

## Data analysis

### Sample description

All baseline demographic and clinical variables were summarized as means ± standard deviations for continuous variables (age, years of education, and device energy) and as group-specific frequencies for categorical variables (sex, study completion, termination phase, and medication types). A series of independent-samples t-tests with Welch’s approximation to the degrees of freedom was used to compare means of continuous variables, and a series of Pearson’s $\chi^2$ tests was used to assess independence of categorical variables across randomization groups.

### Per-protocol analysis

The primary analysis was a per-protocol (PP) analysis that included participants who completed the study protocol in full, including complete data on all outcome measures. Per-protocol average treatment effects (ATEs) and their differences between randomization groups were estimated using a series of mixed ANOVAs, with each outcome measure regressed on randomization group as a between-subject factor, timepoint as a within-subject factor, and their interaction. Decisions about rejection of the null hypothesis of zero mean difference for each of these terms were based on F-tests with p-values adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure [@Benjamini2001] to control the false discovery rate (FDR) at 5% across all outcomes of interest. Thus, effects associated with terms with adjusted p-values^[Following the terminology used by @Benjamini2001, FDR-adjusted p-values are referred to as q-values.] less than .05 were considered statistically significant.

This analysis was followed by inspection of pairwise comparisons between timepoints averaged over randomization groups (main effect of timepoint), between timepoints within each randomization group (simple main effect of timepoint), and between randomization groups within each timepoint (simple main effect of randomization group). The significance threshold within each set of pairwise comparisons (i.e., all comparisons for a given outcome) was based on Holm’s correction for multiple comparisons.

### Modified intention to treat analysis

A modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analysis was conducted on the full sample to evaluate the effect of missingness in the per-protocol analysis. For the mITT analysis, a set of linear mixed-effects models was fitted, with each outcome measure regressed on randomization group, timepoint, and their interaction at the group level (fixed effects), and subject-specific intercepts at the individual level (random effects). Results of these models were analyzed using ANOVAs and pairwise comparisons analogous to the per-protocol analysis, including Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment of ANOVA p-values and Tukey adjustment for multiple comparisons within each set of pairwise comparisons.

### Response and remission rates

Response and remission rates were calculated for timepoints T1 and T2, and the hypothesis that randomization group and response/remission status are independent was tested using Fisher’s exact tests separately for each timepoint. Decisions about rejection of the null hypothesis were based on p-values adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure [@Benjamini2001] to control the FDR at 5% across all outcomes, timepoints, and rate types (response vs. remission).

To describe individual responses to treatment more directly, percentage changes^[Since all outcome measures are scaled such that higher scores indicate more severe depression/anxiety symptoms, percentage change was calculated as $100\times\frac{(Score_{T0}-Score_{T1})}{Score_{T0}}$ (and analogously for T2). Positive values therefore indicate symptom reduction (clinical improvement).] at T1 and T2 relative to T0 were calculated for each participant included in the per-protocol analysis and summarized using means and standard deviations. These percentage changes were used for descriptive purposes only and were not included in any statistical analyses.

### Sensitivity to baseline imbalance

Since baseline symptom levels may differ between groups despite randomization, sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of results to potential baseline imbalance. For each primary PP and mITT model, two baseline-adjusted ANCOVA models were fitted, and their simple main effects of timepoint were directly compared with the primary analyses.

The first ANCOVA consisted of linear mixed-effects models with each outcome regressed on randomization group, post-test timepoint, their interaction, and baseline performance as fixed effects, and subject-specific intercepts as random effects. The second ANCOVA additionally included an interaction between baseline performance and post-test timepoint. In both models, baseline performance was treated as a fixed predictor, and only post-test measurements were treated as outcomes. Timepoint effects were derived from estimated marginal means evaluated at the mean baseline value of each outcome. PP and mITT sensitivity analyses differed only in the sample used for model fitting, with the latter using the full sample.

### Software

All analyses were conducted in R version `r with( version, paste(major,minor,sep=".") )` using package *rstatix* for mixed ANOVAs and *lmer4* with *lmerTest* and *emmeans* for mixed effect models [@rsoft; @Kassambara2023; @Bates2015; @Kuznetsova2017; @Lenth2026]. Computer code to produce presented results is available at [https://github.com/josefmana/deprtms.git](https://github.com/josefmana/deprtms.git).

# Results

```{r}
#| label: desc
N <- d0 |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  pull(n, name = treatment)

age <- d0 |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(
    M = rprint(mean(age), 2),
    range = paste(range(age), collapse = "-"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  add_row(
    treatment = "total",
    M = rprint(mean(d0$age), 2),
    range = paste(range(d0$age), collapse = "-")
  ) |>
  column_to_rownames("treatment")

fem <- d0 |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(
    percfem = paste0(rprint(100 * (table(sex)) |> prop.table(), 0), "%")[1],
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  add_row(
    treatment = "total",
    percfem = paste0(rprint(100 * (table(d0$sex) |> prop.table()), 0), "%")[1]
  ) |>
  pull(percfem, name = treatment)
```

## Participant demographics

`r firstup(as.character(english(sum(N))))` subjects were randomized (mean age = `r age["total", "M"]`; range = `r age["total", "range"]`; `r fem["total"]` females; n = `r N["iTBS"]` in iTBS group; n = `r N["HF-rTMS"]` in the HF-rTMS group). Baseline demographics are presented in @tbl-demo. A flow diagram showing participant progress through the phases of the randomized trial is presented in Figure 1.

We did not detect any statistically significant difference between randomization groups in demographic variables, clinical variables, completion rates or termination phase. The outcome variables are summarized in @tbl-pp-desc for the sample used in the per-protocol analysis and @tbl-itt-desc for the full sample. The data used for the per-protocol analysis are further summarised in @fig-per-protocol.

## Depression outcomes

Results of mixed ANOVAs and pairwise comparisons for depression and anxiety outcomes are summarized in @tbl-pp-aov and @tbl-pp-pwc-occas-main, @tbl-pp-pwc-occas-simp, and @tbl-pp-pwc-treat-simp, respectively. Response and remission rates are presented in @tbl-resp-rates.

Across all depression measures, a statistically significant per-protocol ATE was detected, as indicated by low q-values associated with the timepoint factor (@tbl-pp-aov). This effect was driven by a moderate to large reduction in symptoms from T0 to T1, followed by negligible change from T1 to T2 (@tbl-pp-pwc-occas-main). No statistically significant differences in ATEs between HF-rTMS and iTBS were detected (interaction terms in @tbl-pp-aov and @tbl-pp-pwc-occas-simp). A statistically significant difference between groups was observed for the HAMD subscores “Disturbed Circadian Rhythm” and “Sleep Disorders,” with the iTBS group showing higher symptom levels across timepoints (@tbl-pp-pwc-treat-simp).

The highest response and remission rates among depression measures were observed for HAMD. Distributions of response and remission rates at T1 and T2 were consistent with the null hypothesis of no difference between groups after FDR adjustment (@tbl-resp-rates).

## Anxiety outcomes

Across anxiety outcomes (HAMA, BAI, and PSS), a statistically significant per-protocol ATE was observed (see @tbl-pp-aov), reflecting a pattern similar to that seen in depression outcomes: a reduction in symptoms from T0 to T1 followed by minimal change from T1 to T2 (@tbl-pp-pwc-occas-main).

Importantly, group differences were observed for HAMA outcomes, with the HF-rTMS group showing a more favorable trajectory than the iTBS group. Specifically, the interaction between randomization group and timepoint was statistically significant for HAMA total score and HAMA psychological anxiety (@tbl-pp-aov). In the HF-rTMS group, there was a large reduction in HAMA scores from T0 to T1, which was maintained at T2 (i.e., both T1 and T2 were lower than T0, with no meaningful difference between T1 and T2). In contrast, the iTBS group showed a smaller, although statistically significant, reduction from T0 to T1, followed by no clear difference between T2 and either T0 or T1 (@tbl-pp-pwc-occas-simp).

Response and remission rates for BAI were negligible. In contrast, HAMA response and remission rates ranged from 17.8% to 50.0% and from 68.9% to 88.2%, respectively (@tbl-resp-rates). At T2, response rates for HAMA were higher in the HF-rTMS group than in the iTBS group; however, this difference did not reach statistical significance after FDR adjustment.

## Sensitivity analyses

Results of the mITT analysis are presented in @tbl-itt-aov, @tbl-itt-pwc-occas-main, @tbl-itt-pwc-occas-simp, and @tbl-itt-pwc-treat-simp. Baseline-adjusted simple main effects of timepoint are compared with the primary analyses in @tbl-pp-baseline-sens and @tbl-itt-baseline-sens. Overall, these results were consistent with the primary per-protocol analysis.
